description: Security principles, agent risks, and controls taught by the AI Agent Security Lab.

principles.name: Least Privilege
principles.summary: Give the agent only the minimum permissions needed for the current mission.
principles.details: Every tool and action should be scoped to the smallest set required. When a mission finishes, its elevated permissions should be released. An over-permissioned agent turns a small prompt trick into a large compromise.
principles.good_practice: Bind permissions to a per-mission role and revoke them after execution.

principles.name: Defense in Depth
principles.summary: Layer independent controls so no single failure is catastrophic.
principles.details: Prompt sanitization, output validation, policy checks, and human approval are separate layers. An attacker must defeat them all, not just one.
principles.good_practice: Never rely on a single control; stack independent guardrails.

principles.name: Zero Trust
principles.summary: Treat every tool call, input, and memory read as untrusted until verified.
principles.details: Data returned by tools is untrusted input, not instructions. A document fetched by the agent is data; its embedded 'instructions' are attacks. Memory must be integrity-checked before being relied on.
principles.good_practice: Separate instructions from data at every stage of the loop.

principles.name: Human Approval
principles.summary: High-risk actions require a human to approve before execution.
principles.details: Autonomous agents can act fast and at scale. Gate destructive, irreversible, or data-exposing actions behind an explicit human confirmation.
principles.good_practice: Define a risk threshold above which a human is always in the loop.

principles.name: Tool Allowlist
principles.summary: Only tools on an approved list can be called by the agent.
principles.details: An allowlist is simpler and safer than a denylist: capabilities are added deliberately, never accidentally discovered by the model.
principles.good_practice: Expose a fixed, reviewed tool catalog per environment.

principles.name: Output Validation
principles.summary: Validate the agent's outgoing actions and responses against policy.
principles.details: Before any real action fires, check the resolved tool call, its arguments, and the target. Block calls that violate policy or exceed scope.
principles.good_practice: Treat the final tool invocation as the security-critical boundary.

principles.name: Policy Enforcement
principles.summary: A centralized engine that evaluates every requested action before it runs.
principles.details: The policy engine answers: who is the caller, what action is requested, what permission does it need, and what is the risk. It either allows or blocks with a reason.
principles.good_practice: Log every allow/block decision with the rule that produced it.

principles.name: Expanded Attack Surface
principles.summary: Every tool the agent can call is a new place an attacker can influence.
principles.details: A chatbot only outputs text; an agent reads files, queries systems, and triggers actions. Each tool is a target: its data can be poisoned, its permissions abused, its results trusted too blindly.
principles.good_practice: Model and defend every tool boundary like a network service.

risk_factors.name: Indirect Prompt Injection
risk_factors.description: Malicious instructions hidden in data the agent reads (documents, logs, web pages) override the operator's goal.
risk_factors.why_dangerous: The agent trusts tool output as information, but an attacker uses that same channel to send commands.
risk_factors.control: Prompt sanitization, instruction-vs-data separation, output validation.

risk_factors.name: Memory Poisoning
risk_factors.description: False or attacker-controlled facts stored in agent memory mislead later decisions.
risk_factors.why_dangerous: The agent reuses memory across missions; one poisoned entry can corrupt many future decisions.
risk_factors.control: Memory validation, provenance tracking, integrity checks.

risk_factors.name: Excessive Permissions
risk_factors.description: The agent is granted more privilege than the mission requires.
risk_factors.why_dangerous: A tiny prompt trick then executes with full power instead of a scoped minimum.
risk_factors.control: Least privilege, per-mission roles, permission matrix review.

risk_factors.name: Tool Misuse
risk_factors.description: The agent uses a legitimate tool for an unintended or harmful purpose.
risk_factors.why_dangerous: Tools amplify actions; misuse turns a 'read' capability into data exfiltration or a destructive call.
risk_factors.control: Output validation, action allowlists, human approval on sensitive calls.

risk_factors.name: Goal Manipulation
risk_factors.description: An attacker redefines what the agent thinks it is supposed to achieve.
risk_factors.why_dangerous: The agent optimizes toward the wrong objective and its other defenses can be bypassed by the new framing.
risk_factors.control: Pinned system goal, instruction hierarchy, prompt sanitization.

risk_factors.name: Instruction Override
risk_factors.description: Embedded or spoofed instructions claim higher priority than the operator's original task.
risk_factors.why_dangerous: If the agent believes the attacker's instruction outranks the mission, controls built on the original goal are moot.
risk_factors.control: Instruction hierarchy, policy engine authority, sanitization.

controls.name: Least Privilege
controls.description: Grant tools only for the current mission; revoke when done.

controls.name: Human Approval
controls.description: Require explicit human confirmation for high-risk actions.

controls.name: Prompt Sanitization
controls.description: Strip or neutralize embedded instructions found in tool output.

controls.name: Output Validation
controls.description: Validate each resolved action before it executes.

controls.name: Memory Validation
controls.description: Verify memory entries for provenance and consistency.

controls.name: Tool Allowlist
controls.description: Only pre-approved tools can be invoked.

controls.name: Execution Timeout
controls.description: Bound how long a mission and its tool calls may run.

controls.name: Policy Engine
controls.description: Central allow/block decision maker over every action.

teaching_points.title: Unlike chatbots, AI agents can perform actions.
teaching_points.explanation: A chatbot returns a response. An agent returns actions: it calls tools, reads systems, and changes state. Output is no longer the only risk surface.
teaching_points.key_takeaway: Agent security must protect what the agent does, not just what it says.

teaching_points.title: Every tool increases the attack surface.
teaching_points.explanation: Each tool is a new channel: its inputs can be poisoned, its permissions can be abused, and its output can be trusted too blindly.
teaching_points.key_takeaway: Adding a tool adds a new defensive boundary to design.

teaching_points.title: Agent security depends on architecture, not only prompts.
teaching_points.explanation: Prompt filtering helps, but real safety comes from the runtime: policy engines, allowlists, validation, and human gates around the action loop.
teaching_points.key_takeaway: Hardening the loop is more durable than hardening the wording.

teaching_points.title: Permission boundaries are one of the most important defenses.
teaching_points.explanation: The single biggest amplifier of agent attacks is excessive permission. Narrow, per-mission permissions contain the blast radius of any compromise.
teaching_points.key_takeaway: Least privilege is the first line of defense for autonomous systems.

teaching_points.title: Tool output is data, not instructions.
teaching_points.explanation: A document the agent reads is untrusted input. Its embedded 'instructions' are attacks, no matter how authoritative they sound.
teaching_points.key_takeaway: The agent must treat every observation as data to be validated.
